steps.user_message: I want to file my 2023 taxes correctly. I'm married filing jointly in Chicago IL. W-2 from Midwest Health Systems: $82,350. Additional income: $12,500 (graphic design, 4 clients), $1,560 from Discover Bank savings, $320 from Interactive Brokers. Home office: 130 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,720/month for 780 sq ft. Deductions: $4,100 student loan interest (FedLoan, 2016–2020); $2,000 to St. Mary's Food Bank (have the receipt) have the receipt; $780 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — I can walk you through what’s deductible, whether itemizing makes sense, how to treat the home office, and which forms you’ll need. I’ll also flag a few clarifying questions so I can give exact numbers.

Quick summary (high level)
- Report your W-2 wages ($82,350), interest income (Discover + Interactive Brokers = $1,880), and self-employment income ($12,500) on Form 1040.
- Your self-employment work (graphic design) is reported on Schedule C and subject to self-employment tax (Schedule SE). That makes you eligible for the home-office deduction (if the space is used exclusively and regularly for the business).
- Home-office actual-expense deduction (using your rent allocation) will almost certainly beat the simplified method.
- Student loan interest can be an above-the-line deduction (up to $2,500) if that interest was paid in 2023 and you meet the income limits — based on the income you listed you’re likely eligible, but please confirm the year(s) the $4,100 was paid.
- Charitable donation ($2,000) only helps if you itemize. With the 2023 standard deduction for married filing jointly ($27,700) you most likely will take the standard deduction unless you have substantial other itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, large property taxes, or large state taxes up to the $10,000 SALT cap).
- You’ll likely also be able to claim the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (~20% of qualified business income) because your taxable income will be well below the QBI phase‑out threshold.

Details, calculations, and forms

1) Income to report
- W-2 from Midwest Health Systems: report on Form 1040 (attach W-2 info).
- Self-employment income ($12,500): report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business).
- Interest: Discover $1,560 + Interactive Brokers $320 = $1,880. Report on Form 1040; because combined interest > $1,500 you must file Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
- Any 1099-NEC/1099-MISC from clients: include on Schedule C.

2) Self-employment tax and adjustments
- You’ll calculate net profit on Schedule C (gross self-employment income minus business expenses).
- Self-employment tax (Social Security + Medicare) is computed on Schedule SE; you pay ~15.3% on 92.35% of net self-employment earnings.
- Half of the self-employment tax is deductible as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (so it lowers your AGI).

3) Home office
- You meet the basic test: exclusive and regular business use of 130 sq ft out of 780 total sq ft = 130/780 = 16.67% of the home.
- Two methods:
  - Simplified: $5 per square foot × 130 sq ft = $650 deduction.
  - Actual expenses: allocate a portion of rent, utilities, etc. to the office. With rent $1,720/month → annual rent = $20,640. Allocated portion = 16.67% × $20,640 ≈ $3,440. (If you have utilities/internet you’d allocate the same percent of those amounts to increase the deduction.)
- Because $3,440 >> $650, the actual method (Form 8829) is likely better for you. The amount calculated on Form 8829 flows to Schedule C and reduces net self-employment income (and thus both income tax and self-employment tax).

4) Student loan interest
- Only interest you paid in 2023 qualifies. You should have received Form 1098-E from your servicer for the interest paid in 2023.
- The student loan interest deduction is an adjustment to income (Schedule 1), limited to $2,500 maximum (subject to income phaseouts). Based on the income items you listed, you’re likely under the phaseout and could claim up to $2,500 — but confirm how much interest was actually paid in 2023 (not prior years).

5) Unreimbursed expenses ($780)
- If these are employee unreimbursed business expenses (for a job where you are an employee), those are not deductible for tax years 2018–2025 (suspended miscellaneous itemized deductions).
- If the $780 relates to your self-employment (graphic design) as business expenses, include them on Schedule C and they reduce your net self-employment income.

6) Charitable donation ($2,000)
- Deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Given the 2023 standard deduction for married filing jointly ($27,700), $2,000 by itself won’t make itemizing worthwhile unless you have substantial other itemized deductions (mortgage interest, property taxes, state income taxes up to $10,000 SALT cap, large medical expenses beyond threshold, etc.).

7) Qualified Business Income (QBI)
- With a small net self-employment profit you’ll likely qualify for a 20% QBI deduction (Form 8995 or 8995-A). This is taken after AGI to reduce taxable income and can be significant relative to the small business income.

8) Likely outcome on itemizing vs standard deduction
- Unless you have other large itemizable deductions (mortgage interest, property tax, large SALT up to the $10k cap), the standard deduction for MFJ in 2023 ($27,700) will almost certainly be better than itemizing for the $2,000 charitable gift + limited other items you mentioned. So most likely: take the standard deduction.

9) Forms you’ll need (main ones)
- Form 1040 (U.S. Individual Income Tax Return)
- Schedule 1 (additional income and adjustments: student loan interest adjustment, half SE tax flows on)
- Schedule B (interest) — because total interest > $1,500
- Schedule C (profit or loss from business) — for $12,500 self-employment
- Schedule SE — self-employment tax
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual-expense method for the home office
- Form 1098-E — student loan interest statement (for amounts paid in 2023)
- Form 8995 (Qualified Business Income Deduction) — likely the simplified 8995 if your taxable income is under the threshold
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (unlikely given what you’ve listed)

Records and documents to gather
- W-2 from Midwest Health Systems
- 1099-INT from Discover / Interactive Brokers (or other statements showing interest amounts)
- 1099-NEC/1099-MISC or records of the $12,500 self-employment receipts (bank deposits, invoices)
- Receipts and records for home office (floor plan if helpful), rent statements, utilities if you plan to include them
- 1098-E for student loan interest paid in 2023
- Charitable donation receipt for the $2,000 gift
- Receipts for any business expenses (the $780) if they are business-related

A worked example (approximate) — show impact if self-employment expenses are business-related
- Gross wages: $82,350
- Interest: $1,880
- Self-employment gross: $12,500
- Home-office allocation of rent (actual method): ≈ $3,440
- Other business expenses: $780 (if business related)
- Net business income ≈ $12,500 − $3,440 − $780 = $8,280
- Self-employment tax (approx): ≈ $1,170 → half deductible ≈ $585
- If you can take student loan interest deduction up to $2,500 (and that interest was paid in 2023), subtract that as an adjustment as well.
- AGI and taxable income estimate after the standard deduction would leave you well below the standard-deduction threshold for itemizing benefit — so standard deduction looks best.

Questions I need to confirm to finalize exact numbers
1. Was the $4,100 student loan interest paid in 2023 (i.e., do you have a 2023 Form 1098-E showing that amount)? Only interest paid in tax year 2023 is deductible on your 2023 return.
2. Are the $780 “unreimbursed expenses” employee job expenses (for an employer) or business expenses for your graphic design work? If they are self-employment expenses, they belong on Schedule C and are deductible; if they are employee unreimbursed expenses, they are not deductible (2018–2025 suspension).
3. Do you have other itemizable amounts not listed (mortgage interest, property taxes, separate state tax payments, big medical expenses, etc.) that would push total itemized deductions above $27,700?
4. Do you have any 1099‑NEC payments from clients (or did any client report payments to you on 1099‑NEC)? That won’t change the taxable amount (still included on Schedule C), but it affects recordkeeping and matching.

If you want, I can:
- Run estimated, detailed numbers for your 2023 return if you confirm the answers to the questions above (I can show AGI, taxable income, approximate tax, and the QBI and SE tax calculations).
- Draft a checklist email you can send to yourself listing all documents to collect before filing.
- Or, if you want me to prepare a draft email to your tax preparer with all these facts & numbers, I can draft that for you.

Which of the clarification questions above can you answer now?
